Lessons.Title: Solve Problems
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 Grade5 U06:L12 applies mixed fraction sums and differences in multistep everyday problems, requiring a reasoned estimate as well as exact solution; multiple valid strategies of adding on, common parts, and using the unit whole remain teacher scored.

Warm-up original Estimation Exploration asks3/17+17/19, exact346/323 =1 23/323, close to1 (but no unique low/about-right/high estimates). A source estimate must be described as approximate and pupil generated.

Activity1 Priya's ORIGINAL Salad Dressing Recipe has3/4 cup olive oil,1/3 cup LEMON JUICE,1/2 cup MUSTARD (plus pinch salt/pepper). Priya has2/3 cup olive oil so needs1/12 cup more, which is MORE than1 tablespoon=1/16 cup; therefore one tablespoon alone is NOT enough. Total recipe19/12 =1 7/12 cups, ABOUT1 1/2 cups but not exactly.

Activity2 More Problems To Solve original choice A protein bars: Jada adds1/2+1/3=5/6 cup walnuts; target1 1/3 cups means another1/2 cup. Choice B hike1 1/2+4/10=1 9/10 miles; total trail2 1/2 miles leaves3/5 mile. Both contexts, multiple methods, and partner revision teacher reviewed.

Previous fictional vinegar/citrus recipe and 1 3/4-mile hike are not source; preserve only as clearly optional Edulytiks extensions. Selected exact numeric cases do not score pupil explanations or optional activities.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: use different strategies to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators in MULTI-STEP real-world situations, estimate reasonableness and explain each step in context. The 2021 source's salad dressing task also asks whether the estimate means exactly or about a given amount.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: compare 2/3 and3/4 using twelfths; both are less than one cup but together exceed one. Discuss whether a recipe total must be exact and which estimates convey enough useful precision.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — original recipe: combine 3/4 cup oil,1/3 cup vinegar and1/6 cup citrus. Convert to twelfths 9/12+4/12+2/12=15/12=1 1/4 cups. If the cook has a 1 1/2-cup bottle, 1/4 cup of capacity remains. Compare 'about one and a quarter' with an exact expression; a learner must justify a plausible estimate before computation.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — choose one context: hiker A travels 1 3/4 miles, then2/5 mile; the total is43/20=2 3/20 miles. If the route is 3 miles, 17/20 mile remains. In another original food task, 1/2 cup nuts plus1/3 cup nuts makes5/6 cup; to reach1 1/4 cups the cook needs5/12 cup more. Partners explain which equations represent each stage and why their units remain consistent.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: source asks for estimation, explaining recipe quantities and two alternate story solutions. A numeric answer cannot auto-pass whether an estimate is reasonable or a partner communicated the context faithfully.

Lessons.Title: Put It All Together: Add and Subtract Fractions
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L13 considers MULTIPLE common denominators and why proposed denominators18,24,48 do or do not work for denominators6 and8. Pupils choose any valid efficient strategy and justify equivalence.
Warm-up original source1/8+5/8=3/4,1/8+6/16=1/2,1/8+1/3=11/24,1/8+5/12=13/24. Students can represent these values with common units or an area model.

Activity1 original source fraction4/6+5/8=2/3+5/8=31/24=1 7/24. Tyler claims18 common denominator INVALID because18 not multiple8. Han24 and Clare48 both VALID; using24 gives16/24+15/24=31/24, 48 gives32/48+30/48=62/48=31/24. Previous invented2/3+3/8 is not the source expression.
Activity2 original source2/5+13/15=19/15,6/5−1/3=13/15,11/12+3 5/9=4 17/36 and6/10−9/25=6/25. Verify a denominator common to original pair, and discuss if there is a smaller convenient multiple.

All source teacher visual representations, critique of Tyler/Han/Clare and choice of denominator are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED; selected numeric exact cases test original sums only. Independent Edulytiks Cool-down is distinct from publisher original.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: critique claims about common denominators, distinguish invalid choices from two valid choices, and flexibly select convenient equivalent forms to add and subtract fractions. The original source contrasts denominators 18,24 and48 for6ths and8ths.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: list multiples of6 and8. The first positive common multiple is24; 48 is also a common multiple, while18 is not divisible by8. Explain why using18 would force non-integer rescaling of eighths, so it cannot be the common denominator in the usual equivalent-fraction strategy.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — critique three learners: find 2/3+3/8. One student proposes denominator18, another24, another48. Denominator18 is not a multiple of8; 24 gives16/24+9/24=25/24;48 gives32/48+18/48=50/48=25/24. Students explain why both24 and48 work but24 is simpler.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — compare strategies: find 3/5+4/15 using fifteenths to get9/15+4/15=13/15. Find6/5−1/3 as18/15−5/15=13/15. For 4/7+5/6, denominator42 yields24/42+35/42=59/42. A partner chooses another valid common multiple and explains why the quotient stays equal.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: the source asks whom the student agrees with, alternative denominator choices and written critique. Correct numeric sums are supporting evidence only; the reasons given for accepting or rejecting a denominator need teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Common denominator test
KeyConcepts.Definition: A common denominator is a positive multiple of every original denominator.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 24 and48 are multiples of6 and8;18 is not.

KeyConcepts.Title: Two valid equivalent calculations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Changing numerator and denominator together preserves amount.

KeyConcepts.Title: Choosing an efficient scale
KeyConcepts.Definition: The least common multiple is often simpler than the full denominator product.

Lessons.Title: Representing Fractions on a Line Plot
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L14 constructs and interprets a LINE PLOT using egg weight fractions in EIGHTHS. Frequency and equivalent labels matter; source paper graph, student construction and interpretation beyond bounded counts are TEACHER_REVIEW_REQUIRED.

Warm-up Which One Doesn't Belong Line Plot A/B/C/D source pictures are not fully readable as standalone numeric records from HTML. Teacher assesses pupil's own valid distinctions without inventing publisher exact axis labels.

Activity1 Sums of Fractions spinner game asks partners to spin twice, ADD fractional outcomes, record ONE summed point, repeat until TWELVE data points in their personally collected line plot. Teacher scores real rolls, max−min and discussion; there is no single fixed original spinner dataset.

Activity2 Lots of Eggs original printed TWELVE weights 1 7/8,2 1/2,2 3/8,1 3/4,2 1/4,2 4/8,2 1/8,1 7/8,2 1/4,1 6/8,2 1/8,1 7/8 ounces. Equivalent labels2 4/8=2 1/2 and1 6/8=1 3/4 must share same line-plot tick. Frequencies:1 3/4 twice,1 7/8 three,2 1/8 twice,2 1/4 twice,2 3/8 once,2 1/2 twice. So Jada's claim1/4 of eggs are1 7/8oz TRUE (3/12), and heaviest2 1/2 minus lightest1 3/4=3/4oz.

Prior fictitious fruit/egg plots remain optional Edulytiks examples and not the source plot. Exact numeric choices cover only source egg metrics; original plotted X positions, Jada's fraction proof, spinner results require human rubric.

Source and assessment limits: independently authored Edulytiks Cool-down with teacher-reviewed drawing/explanation. Original publisher gated Cool-down, standalone student PDF and original image binaries are not individually certified. Numeric exact choices cover only eligible subskills, not the original open source tasks.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Goal: construct, label and INTERPRET a line plot with fractional values in halves, quarters and eighths, and use fraction addition on a partner spinner's actual outcomes. The original lesson has a physical two-spin game and then a line plot of measured egg weights. A calculation alone cannot substitute for recording real outcomes.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Warm-up: draw an original number line from zero to two with eighth-sized tick marks. Ask students where 1/4,1/2,3/4,1 1/8 and1 7/8 sit and require equal spacing. Mark numbers first, then X's for repeated values.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 1 — first-party simulation demonstration only: spinner fractions are1/4,1/2,3/4. In five hypothetical two-spin rounds choose (1/4,1/2), (1/2,1/2), (1/4,3/4), (3/4,3/4), (1/2,3/4). Totals are3/4,1,1,1 1/2,1 1/4, giving one X at3/4, two at1, one at1 1/4 and one at1 1/2. The authentic task still requires learner-generated spinner outcomes; hypothetical outcomes are not scored as real student records.

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Activity 2 — egg weights example: a fictional collection of eight eggs has weights1 1/2,1 5/8,1 5/8,1 3/4,1 7/8,1 7/8,1 7/8,2 ounces. Label a line plot from1 1/2 to2 in eighths. There are three eggs at1 7/8, or3/8 of the egg count, while each weighs1 7/8 ounces. Distinguish 'three eighths of the eggs' (fraction of count) from 'one and seven eighths ounces' (measurement).

Optional previous source-aligned or independently authored extension — Teacher boundary: students physically spin, choose the plot scale, construct X stacks, and critique a statement mixing weight fractions and count fractions. These drawings, observation data and explanations are teacher-reviewed; numerical counts alone are only subchecks.

KeyConcepts.Title: Line plot labels and X counts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each X represents one observed or simulated datum, plotted over its exact fractional measurement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Five rounds give two X's at one whole and one X at three other totals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction of observations vs measured fraction
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction of a dataset's COUNT differs from a fractional measurement.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 3/8 of eggs by count weigh1 7/8 ounces each.
KeyConcepts.Example: These two fractions refer to different wholes.

KeyConcepts.Title: Add spin fractions with common parts
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each round's total is the sum of two independently selected fractional positions.
KeyConcepts.Example: The plot labels that exact point.

Lessons.Title: Problem Solving with Line Plots
ExplanationParagraphs: Original IM2021 G5 U06:L15 uses an INFO GAP: one student receives a problem card, the other a data card and they may NOT show/read each other the card. Student asks mathematical questions to recover necessary data; no fixed card answers can be certified from unavailable source card images.
Warm-up Multiply by18 printed1/3×18=6,2/3×18=12,4/3×18=24,5/3×18=30; these model repeated addition and distributive fraction multiplication.

Activity1 Info Gap Picking Fruit requires an actual teacher-supplied problem card and data card, respectful spoken questions, repeated role reversal and teacher checking. The source images/text do not expose full paired card data. Earlier independently-authored six-apricot toy exercise is an optional Edulytiks DEMO, never the original hidden card set.

Optional Activity2 Mathematical Questions has original HTML alt-described Mai's Apricots line plot starting at7/8oz, then thirteen eighth ticks with frequencies [1,0,2,0,0,2,5,3,1,0,0,0,1], totaling FIFTEEN apricots. KeyConcepts.Title: Missing observations prevent unique findings
KeyConcepts.Definition: An incomplete line plot cannot determine a mode, maximum or total without the relevant missing data.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Request exact missing weights or frequencies before drawing conclusions.
KeyConcepts.Example: The information gap is the core source task.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fractional plot frequencies
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each X contributes exactly one fruit at the labeled weight.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Two values at1 1/4 and two at1 3/4 create a two-way tie for mode.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not invent a single mode.

KeyConcepts.Title: Weighted total
KeyConcepts.Definition: The total mass is the sum of (weight×frequency) across all labels.
KeyConcepts.Example: One pound equals16oz in the mass context.

Lessons.Title: Compare Products
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare a positive quantity multiplied by a fraction less than one, equal to one or greater than one WITHOUT treating every comparison as a long arithmetic problem. The 2021 source presents physical trail-distance fractions and asks children to construct their OWN valid fractions in inequalities.

Warm-up: picture a six-mile trail with a marked portion shorter than the whole. A one-half factor selects3 miles; a five-fourths factor selects a distance extending past the original six-mile path if the context permits. Explain the difference between a fraction of a whole and distance beyond the original trail.

Activity 1 — trail fractions: compare5/6 of a six-mile trail with7/6 of the same trail. The first is5 miles, the second7 miles, but the main conceptual evidence is that5/6<1 and7/6>1. Now compare three runners taking1/2,3/4 and5/4 of a four-mile route; predict ordering from fractions before computing2,3,5 miles.

Activity 2 — choose a numerator: complete n/9×36<36 with several valid positive integer numerators n=1,4,8; choose n=9 to obtain equality and n=10 to exceed36. Explain why ANY proper positive fraction reduces the value of a positive fixed whole, but changing signs or zero requires separate analysis not supplied by the original context.

Teacher boundary: source requires comparisons, a chosen missing numerator and explanatory claims about multiplier size, including drawings or partner dialogue. Numeric distances are supporting checks; teacher reviews the mathematical generalization.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction below one shrinks a positive factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: For a positive a, multiplying by positive f<1 yields 0<fa<a.
KeyConcepts.Example: Fewer than all equal parts of a full distance.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction above one increases positive factor
KeyConcepts.Definition: A positive fraction greater than one produces a product above the original positive quantity.

KeyConcepts.Title: One is unchanged
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiplying by one preserves the original quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: A numerator matching positive denominator selects the whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compare without calculation
WorkedExamples.Question: Order1/2,3/4,5/4 of a positive four-mile route.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party mathematically equivalent model; human reviews drawings, communication and choices.
Steps: Compare the fractions to one and to each other.
Use their order1/2<3/4<5/4.
Multiply four by each only as confirmation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the comparison argument.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose several valid fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Find positive integer n such that n/9×36<36.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party mathematically equivalent model; human reviews drawings, communication and choices.
Steps: Recognize n/9 must be below one.
Choose n between1 and8 inclusive.
Give several examples and contrast n=9, n=10.
WorkedExamples.Check: n=9 yields36; n=10 yields40.

WorkedExamples.Title: Above-one fraction
WorkedExamples.Question: Find7/6 of a six-mile course.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party mathematically equivalent model; human reviews drawings, communication and choices.
Steps: Recognize7/6=1+1/6.
Compute one whole six miles plus one more sixth of it.
Compare with the original six.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Claim multiplication always makes a positive number bigger
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A factor below one produces a smaller positive result.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare multiplier with one before predicting size.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Select only one valid numerator when the task permits many
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Several fractions below one satisfy the inequality.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State a valid range and illustrate multiple choices.

SummaryPoints: The multiplier's relationship to one predicts the size of a positive product.
Original contexts often allow multiple correct fraction choices.
Teacher reviews fractional diagrams and generalization reasoning.
